trial_050_result.diagnostic: Ran experiments/scripts/diagnostic_eval_stage2.py (locally, CPU, ~2000 val examples) on the trial-050 checkpoint to check for real per-label ranking signal underneath the threshold. Result: median per-label AUROC=0.8366 (mean 0.8283), 87.3% of the 362 evaluable labels have AUROC>0.7. Pooled @ threshold 0.5: precision=0.6565, recall=0.4583, F1=0.5398 (vs. trivial baseline accuracy 0.9643). Best pooled F1 over a threshold sweep: 0.5727 @ threshold=0.32. This is a genuinely well-performing model, not a collapsed one.
trial_050_result.root_cause_found_and_fixed: training_run.py's compute_metrics() computed per-batch recall (tp/(tp+fn)) and averaged those ratios across batches. With batch_size=8 and 383 labels at 3.58% positive rate, the expected positive count for any given label in an 8-example batch is ~0.29 - meaning the overwhelming majority of (label, batch) pairs have zero true positives, so tp/(tp+fn+eps)=0 for most labels in most batches regardless of model quality, dragging every batch's (and therefore the epoch's) averaged recall toward 0. This is a ratio-aggregation error (average-of-ratios != ratio-of-sums), not present for accuracy (a linear average, aggregates correctly regardless of batching) - only recall was affected. Confirmed via a synthetic test: a model constructed to have true recall=1.0 was reported as 25.7% recall under the old per-batch-averaging code, 100% under the fix. Fixed by having compute_metrics() return raw per-batch counts (correct/total/tp/fn) and adding finalize_metrics() to accumulate those across a full epoch before computing the final ratio once - applied to both the training and validation loops. Prior trials (3-label task) were only mildly affected by this bug, since 3 sparse-but-not-this-sparse labels rarely hit zero-positives-per-8-example-batch the way 383 labels do; not worth re-running them retroactively.
trial_050_result.implication: val_loss (never affected by this bug) remains the trustworthy metric across the whole sweep, old and new phases alike. val_recall/train_recall going forward (trial-051+) will now be computed correctly and should be trusted; anything before this fix (all of trial-001 through trial-050) has recall numbers that undersold real model quality on sparse/high-label-count tasks, worst for trial-050 specifically.

pos_weight_feature.why: trial-050's diagnostic showed a real, if moderate, threshold-calibration issue from class imbalance: best F1 (0.5727) came at threshold=0.32, not 0.5, and recall@0.5 was only 45.8% - unweighted BCE naturally pushes predicted probabilities low when negatives vastly outnumber positives (3.58% overall). pos_weight counteracts this by upweighting the loss contribution from positive-label mistakes, per label.
pos_weight_feature.implementation: New --pos-weight flag (BooleanOptionalAction, default False) on training_run.py. When set, computes per-label sqrt(n_negative/n_positive) from the training split's label_counts (already computed for bias-init, now hoisted out of the resume-from-revision conditional so it's always available) and passes it as BCEWithLogitsLoss's pos_weight tensor. sqrt chosen over raw inverse-frequency after checking the real distribution: raw ratio spans 0.38-4780.7 across the 383 labels (~12,600x, would cause gradient spikes whenever a rare positive appears in a batch), sqrt compresses this to 0.61-69.14 (~113x) while staying well-behaved at both ends with no clamp/floor needed (unlike a naive log2 formula, which goes negative for the majority-positive aspect roots). Verified: pos_weight tensor shape/values match the hand-computed distribution exactly, BCEWithLogitsLoss accepts and broadcasts it correctly against [batch, 383] targets, CLI flag parses correctly.
pos_weight_feature.trial: trial-051 (experiments/round8_manifest.json / experiments/round8_manual.ipynb) - isolated A/B against trial-050, identical config with only --pos-weight added, to get a clean read before folding into a broader round.
pos_weight_feature.device_bug_hit_and_fixed: First attempt crashed: 'Expected all tensors to be on the same device'. Root cause was in the compute_metrics()/finalize_metrics() refactor from the trial-050 analysis, not the pos_weight code - train_metrics_acc/validation_metrics_acc initialized their tp/fn accumulator tensors with plain torch.zeros(len(label_names)) (CPU by default), while compute_metrics()'s per-batch outputs live on whatever device logits/labels are on (cuda during real training). Missed in local testing since this sandbox has no CUDA - every tensor happened to be CPU on both sides there. Fixed by passing device=device to both torch.zeros(...) calls; round8_manual.ipynb was regenerated (it embeds training_run.py's source directly) and resent before trial-051 actually ran.

result.status: complete - negative result for pos_weight as formulated

result.interpretation: pos_weight's mechanism worked exactly as designed: median AUROC ticked up slightly (real ranking-quality improvement) and the optimal classification threshold recalibrated back toward 0.5 (0.32->0.48), confirming it counteracts the low-probability bias from class imbalance as intended. Both trials used identical seed=42, so this isn't seed noise - sqrt(n_neg/n_pos) as formulated overcorrects on this dataset.

implementation.training_run.py: Added --use-lora (peft LoraConfig, target_modules default query,value, modules_to_save=[classifier]), --lora-r/--lora-alpha/--lora-dropout/--lora-target-modules, --mixed-precision {no,fp16,bf16} (autocast + GradScaler for fp16, also controls the dtype the frozen LoRA base loads in), --gradient-checkpointing (with the peft-required model.enable_input_require_grads()). New robust helpers get_classifier_bias_param()/set_classifier_dropout() locate the classifier by parameter/module-name suffix instead of a hardcoded attribute chain, since peft's modules_to_save wrapping restructures the attribute path in a version-dependent way. resume_from_revision is LoRA-aware: a --use-lora checkpoint on --hf-repo-id is adapter-only, so the base architecture always loads fresh from --model-name, with adapter weights attached separately via PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, hf_repo_id, revision=...) rather than treating the checkpoint repo as a loadable full model.
implementation.verification: Structurally verified against a REAL peft 0.19.1 install (user had it available locally + confirmed Colab has the same version pre-installed, so no version-skew risk) using a tiny esm2_t6_8M model: found and fixed a real bug where the initial name-suffix assumption for the bias-init helper didn't match peft's actual wrapping (classifier.modules_to_save.default.out_proj.bias, not classifier.out_proj.bias) - caught locally before it could have silently corrupted bias-init on a real paid GPU run. Also found and fixed that peft upcasts LoRA adapter weights to fp32 automatically when the frozen base loads in bf16, but does NOT do this for the modules_to_save classifier copy (it silently inherits bf16) - create_esm now explicitly upcasts the classifier back to fp32 after wrapping. Verified end-to-end: forward+backward produces real gradients on both LoRA and classifier params, gradient checkpointing doesn't break backprop, save_pretrained produces a small adapter-only checkpoint (~544KB for the tiny test model), and PeftModel.from_pretrained reload is byte-exact (torch.allclose, atol=1e-5) against the pre-save model in eval mode. The non-LoRA (existing sweep) code path was also re-tested after the shared helper-function refactor to confirm no regression.
implementation.diagnostic_eval_stage2.py: Generalized to auto-detect model_name/use_lora by reading trial_metrics.json (already pushed alongside every checkpoint by push_checkpoint(), contains the full CLI config) instead of hardcoding MODEL_NAME='facebook/esm2_t12_35M_UR50D' - works unmodified for any future trial's config, LoRA or not.

results.throughput_comparison: 0.0411s/example at esm2_t12_35M scale (trial-053, no LoRA, no mixed precision, no checkpointing, average of its 10 epochs: 575.4s/14000 examples) vs 5.6843s/example here (1705.3s/300 examples) - a 138x slowdown per example, far more than the ~81x parameter-count ratio (2.85B/35M) alone would predict.
results.budget_implication: At this throughput, a wall-clock budget similar to the 35M sweep's ~10min/epoch would only afford ~150 examples/epoch (30min->~317, 60min->~633, 90min->~950) - nowhere near the 12,000/epoch used throughout the whole esm2_t12_35M_coarse_go_terms phase. This directly conflicts with the ProtBERT-comparison finding that motivated this phase in the first place (more data exposure mattered) - LoRA solved the VRAM constraint but did NOT solve the compute constraint, since forward/backward FLOPs scale with the full frozen backbone regardless of how few parameters are trainable.

trial_067.unexplained_gap_hypothesis: 138x actual vs ~81x parameter-ratio-only expectation - the remaining ~1.7x is plausibly gradient_checkpointing's recompute overhead (commonly costs ~20-40% more backward-pass compute, trading compute for memory) plus other hardware/kernel-efficiency factors not yet isolated. Given v1/v2 smoke tests showed only ~9.5GB peak VRAM usage against a 22.5GB budget - more than 2x headroom unused - gradient_checkpointing may not even be necessary at this batch size, and turning it off is the most promising, cheap, single-variable lever to test for recovering meaningful throughput before accepting this budget as final.
trial_067.next_step: User chose option (a) --no-gradient-checkpointing, and separately asked whether the frozen backbone could be split off entirely (run once with no gradients, only backprop through a trainable tail) - verified directly against peft 0.19.1 that this is real and implementable via LoraConfig's layers_to_transform (not automatic under the current all-layers-targeted config, matching what the user already expected): restricting adapters to only the last N layers means the earlier layers' output activations have requires_grad=False, so PyTorch's autograd builds no backward graph for them at all. Implemented as --lora-layers-to-transform. Combined both changes into trial-068 (see below) given cost - testing each in isolation wasn't worth the extra 3B-scale spend when both are well-understood in direction.

trial_068.purpose: Throughput calibration, round 2. Combines two changes at once (not isolated - see cost rationale below): --no-gradient-checkpointing (both smoke tests showed only ~9.5GB peak VRAM against the 22.5GB budget with checkpointing on, so its memory savings likely aren't needed at batch=8) and --lora-layers-to-transform 18 (restricts LoRA to the last half of the 36 layers, so autograd skips the backward pass entirely for the earlier half - verified directly, see the esm2_t36_3B_lora_scaleup phase's implementation notes). Same batch_size=8 and data budget (200 train/100 val, 1 epoch) as trial-067 for a direct epoch-time comparison, even though the two simultaneous changes won't cleanly separate which contributed how much - a 3B trial's cost wasn't judged worth spending on isolating each variable separately when both are well-understood in direction (both should help, only magnitude was unknown).
trial_068.vram_risk: Removing gradient_checkpointing could increase activation memory substantially, since that's precisely what checkpointing trades away for compute. Untested combination - if this OOMs, the fallback is restoring checkpointing and/or lowering batch_size.

round_1.batch_size_finding: Bigger batch (128) gave the sweep's best val_loss despite ~94 opt steps/epoch (16x fewer than batch=8's 1500), but did NOT speed up wall-clock - batch=8 ran ~530-540s/epoch, batch=32 ~680s/epoch, batch=128 ~735s/epoch, the opposite of the usual larger-batch-is-faster expectation. Likely cause (code-level, not batch-size-inherent): data_collate_function pads each batch to its own longest sequence with no length-bucketing, and shuffle=True draws batches randomly - larger batches have a higher chance of containing a near-max_length (1024) outlier, forcing more padding waste as batch size grows. Not fixed as part of this round; would need length-bucketed batching in training_run.py to actually test batch size's effect on throughput cleanly.
round_1.gpu_memory_observations: User reports trial-033 (batch_size=128, grad_accum_steps=1) almost OOM'd the T4; trial-034 (batch_size=128, grad_accum_steps=4, run immediately after) was surprisingly easier on memory. Per training_run.py (create_esm/DataLoader), grad_accum_steps does NOT reduce per-step batch size - the DataLoader batch_size is used as-is every micro-step, so trial-034 processes full batches of 128 exactly like trial-033; the code gives no mechanism for grad_accum alone to lower peak memory. Most likely explanation: CUDA's caching allocator already expanded its pool to fit batch=128 during trial-033, so trial-034 (running right after, same session) reused that already-grown pool instead of needing to allocate further - an artifact of run order within one session, not a real property of grad_accum_steps. Don't read 'higher grad_accum = lower memory' as a real effect without a controlled A/B (same batch size, accum vs no-accum, in fresh sessions on both sides).

dataset_expansion.status: generate_dataset.py rewritten and dry-run verified against real data; NOT yet regenerated/pushed (awaiting go-ahead) and training_run.py NOT yet updated to match the new schema
dataset_expansion.why: The whole sweep above (both phases) optimized training_run.py's current label space - the 3 top-level GO aspects (C/F/P) - a heavy simplification of the actual CAFA task. generate_dataset.py computes unique_go_terms from train_terms.tsv but discards it, building label2id from unique_aspects instead. Likely explains why the aspect-only task plateaus so early: 3 classes carries very little information for the model to differentiate proteins by, regardless of hyperparameters.
candidate_approaches: Coarse-to-fine curriculum: keep the aspect head as stage 1 (already tuned), add a term-level head as stage 2, fine-tuned from the stage-1 checkpoint, using aspect predictions as an auxiliary signal

Frequency-filtered flat multi-label term set (e.g. terms with >=50-100 annotations, ~700-1600 terms) instead of all 26,125 - standard CAFA-baseline move, needs positive-class weighting or focal loss given ~6.5 positives per protein
True-path-rule-aware loss/label propagation: exploit the GO DAG so rare specific terms borrow gradient signal from their much more frequent ancestors
Switch tracked metrics toward the real CAFA Fmax (using IA.tsv, already in the data dir but unused) instead of threshold-0.5 accuracy/val_loss, once past aspect-only prediction
dataset_expansion.recommended_first_step: Coarse-to-fine curriculum (approach 1) combined with a frequency-filtered term subset (approach 2) as stage 2's label space; true-path-rule loss (approach 3) as a follow-up once basic term-level training is validated. Requires a generate_dataset.py change to build a term-level label space before anything is testable - a bigger lift than another hyperparameter trial, sequenced after this round_3 close-out rather than alongside it.

stage1_diagnostic.status: complete - result: aspect model has real, if modest, discriminative signal - not a dead end
stage1_diagnostic.why: compute_metrics() only tracks accuracy/recall, both of which a trivial 'always predict positive' baseline would already score ~0.698 accuracy / 1.0 recall (the average label prior C=0.716/F=0.685/P=0.693) - suspiciously close to what every trial in the whole sweep has reported (val_acc 0.69-0.70, val_recall usually 0.94-0.99+). Can't tell from existing logs whether the aspect model learned real per-protein signal or just the prior.
stage1_diagnostic.evaluates: kelmoir/cafa6-esm@trial-038, epoch-10 weights (checkpoint_mode=final only ever saves the last epoch, not trial-038's reported-best epoch 7/val_loss 0.5891 - epoch 10 was val_loss 0.5948). Still representative for a yes/no signal question.
stage1_diagnostic.metrics: per-aspect and macro accuracy/precision/recall/F1 at threshold 0.5, best-F1 over a threshold sweep, and AUROC - all reported alongside the analytically-known trivial baseline (accuracy=prior, precision=prior, recall=1.0, AUROC=0.5). AUROC is the key number: close to 0.5 means no real per-protein discriminative signal; clearly above it means the model learned something real even if 0.5-threshold accuracy looks unimpressive.
stage1_diagnostic.bug_fixed_along_the_way: create_esm()'s AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(..., revision=...) call has no explicit token= param, and get_hf_token() never sets os.environ['HF_TOKEN'] after resolving one - so loading a private Hub checkpoint via --resume-from-revision has no real auth path in training_run.py today. Worked around locally in the diagnostic script (os.environ['HF_TOKEN'] = token before calling create_esm); not yet fixed in training_run.py itself since it hasn't visibly broken the CLI self-healing retry path that also uses --resume-from-revision - worth revisiting if that path ever needs it.

results.interpretation: AUROC is clearly above 0.5 for every aspect (0.61-0.68, macro 0.64) - the model has learned real per-protein discriminative signal, not just the label prior. This resolves the 'is it a dead end' question from before: it's not. Nuance worth keeping in mind though: at the standard 0.5 threshold, F1 doesn't clearly beat the trivial baseline (and is slightly worse for F/P) - AUROC (ranking ability, threshold-independent) and F1-at-a-fixed-threshold tell different stories here, because F1 rewards the trivial baseline's perfect recall in a way that undersells the model's real but modest ranking improvement. accuracy/recall alone (the only two metrics compute_metrics() has ever tracked) would never have surfaced this - they sat right on top of the trivial baseline the whole sweep, which is exactly why this diagnostic was worth running before deciding whether Stage 1 was usable.

stage1_diagnostic.user_caveat_2026-07-27: The aspect-only model (AUROC 0.61-0.68, modest but real) could plausibly be trained to genuinely useful quality - IF sequence input actually carries enough real signal for this task at all - but getting there would require substantially more data and training than the current sweep's scale (12,000 train samples, 6-10 epochs, small ESM-2 variants). Not pursued for now; noted as a live possibility rather than a closed question, separate from and prior to the coarse-to-fine dataset expansion below.

ancestor_propagation_check.method: 500 randomly sampled proteins (seed=42) from train_terms.tsv; for each, computed the full true-path ancestor closure of its listed terms via networkx over the obonet-parsed go-basic.obo graph, then checked what fraction of that closure is already present as explicit rows for that protein.
ancestor_propagation_check.result: Only 2.27% of implied ancestor annotations (450 of 19,813) are already explicit in train_terms.tsv; 97.73% are missing. Every single sampled protein (500/500) had at least one missing ancestor annotation; mean per-protein missing fraction was 98.2%.
ancestor_propagation_check.conclusion: train_terms.tsv lists close to only the most-specific asserted annotations, not the propagated closure. Ancestor propagation (via the obonet graph) is NOT optional for any term-level label space - without it, virtually every candidate depth<=2 term (see real_task_stats) would have its positive examples massively undercounted, since most proteins' coarse-level annotations exist only implicitly through their deeper, more specific terms.

findings: go-basic.obo has 5 relationship types: is_a (62,410 edges), part_of (6,597), regulates (2,989), positively_regulates (2,619), negatively_regulates (2,614). Only is_a/part_of support the true-path rule (regulates does not mean is-a-kind-of/part-of) - restricting propagation to those two changes the ancestor-completeness result only marginally (97.65% missing vs. 97.73% with all 5 edge types), but is still the methodologically correct restriction going forward.
0 of 26,125 terms used in train_terms.tsv are missing/obsolete relative to this go-basic.obo - fully version-consistent, no ambiguity from a stale ontology file.
0 of 77,229 edges cross between the C/F/P namespaces - the 3 aspects stay cleanly disjoint.

Depth is convention-dependent: shortest-path vs longest-path depth disagree for 61% of a 2000-term sample, by 1.73 levels on average, up to 10 in the worst case. The ancestor/descendant SET itself is exact and deterministic once edge types are fixed - only the scalar 'depth' summary is ambiguous. Resolved by committing explicitly to shortest-path depth throughout.
